source: Heuer (1999) Psychology of Intelligence Analysis, ch. 8 Analysis of Competing Hypotheses (step 3)
finding: Founding statement of diagnosticity for analysts. Step 3 is called the most important step. The analyst works across the matrix rows, one evidence item at a time, and asks how consistent it is with each hypothesis. Evidence consistent with all hypotheses has no diagnostic value.
numbers: Eight-step procedure. Cell codes are C, I, N/A or plus/minus. Optional refinement: for each cell ask 'if this hypothesis is true, what is the probability I would see this evidence?'
quote: If an item of evidence seems consistent with all the hypotheses, it may have no diagnostic value.
limits: Heuer never tested ACH empirically (see Mandel and Tetlock 2018). The matrix is a notation, not a formula. The numeric-probability version is only an optional refinement.
agent_relevance: S7 should score each candidate test by how differently the rival hypotheses predict it, not by how well it fits the favourite.

source: Heuer (1999) ch. 8, steps 4 to 6 and summary
finding: Step 4 deletes items with no diagnostic value. Step 5 ranks hypotheses by the fewest inconsistent items, not the most consistent ones. Step 6 re-checks the few high-diagnosticity items that drive the result, including a deception check.
numbers: More than seven hypotheses may be unmanageable, so group them. Example matrix: E1 (public statement) consistent with all, no value; E4 diagnostic; E6 double minus is a linchpin.
quote: The hypothesis with the fewest minuses is probably the most likely one.
limits: Counting minuses is a rough rank only: a single inconsistency symbol hides degrees of inconsistency. The same chapter says the matrix must not dictate the answer.
agent_relevance: Matches our rule 'revise from real output': keep a short list of linchpin evidence and re-test exactly those. Code can drop rows whose predictions are identical across candidates.

source: Heuer (1999) ch. 4 Strategies for Analytical Judgment, 'Failure to consider diagnosticity' and the Wason 2-4-6 account
finding: Heuer uses a high-temperature example (sick, but not which illness) and the Wason 2-4-6 task to argue that confirming evidence is cheap when it fits many hypotheses. He applies this to early-warning indicators that also fit a bluff.
numbers: Wason 2-4-6: 6 of 29 subjects were right the first time they announced a rule. In a repeat by another researcher, 0 of 51 were right first time.
quote: The correct rule was any three ascending numbers, either odd or even.
limits: Wason's sequences give deterministic yes/no feedback. Analysts get probabilistic evidence, so one item rarely eliminates a hypothesis (Heuer says this himself). The 'confirmation bias' reading of 2-4-6 is itself contested (see a26).
agent_relevance: Concrete failure to test for: the agent picks probes that its current guess passes. S7 needs probes where the guess and a rival disagree.

source: Heuer (1999) ch. 5/6, correlation study with nurses as cited (Smedslund-style)
finding: Heuer cites a study where nurses judged whether symptom A predicts diagnosis F from 100 cards. Most used only the present-present cell. This is the 2x2 table version of ignoring diagnosticity: a likelihood needs both P(E|H) and P(E|not H).
numbers: 18 of 19 subjects given a zero-correlation deck saw at least a weak relation. More than half used only the A-and-F cell. Of 86 subjects over several runs, none showed intuitive understanding of correlation.
limits: Heuer's summary of an older study (second hand). In the deck, 25 cards had both A and F and 25 had A without F.
agent_relevance: Direct analogue of pseudodiagnosticity: a model given only P(E|H) cannot judge the evidence. The scaffold should force the paired question P(E|H1) versus P(E|H2) before any score.

source: Karvetski and Mandel (2020) Coherence of probability judgments from uncertain evidence: does ACH help? JDM 15(6)
finding: Randomised test of ACH vs no technique on probability judgments from uncertain evidence. ACH gave no gain on any coherence measure. Both groups were subadditive, unreliable and conservative. Only the ACH group showed pseudo-diagnostic weighting.
numbers: N=227 (Qualtrics panel, degree-holders, mean age 40.7), between-subjects. Six cases in three isomorphic pairs: background check plus two informants with NATO-style reliability/credibility codes. Choice-probability match .74. Reliability MAD ACH .22 vs control .18, F=3.86, p=.05, d=0.20 (favours control). Bayesian-coherence agreement .65, d=0.06. Conservatism: Bayesian MAD from 50/50 .33 vs elicited .13, d=1.54.
limits: Hypothetical graffiti-suspect task with only two hypotheses (gang member vs street artist). Per-cell n not reported. Degrees of freedom reported inconsistently (t(218) vs N=227). Not trained analysts.
agent_relevance: A consistency matrix filled by a judge (human or model) can add noise instead of removing it. Let code compute diagnosticity from stated likelihoods.

source: Karvetski and Mandel (2020), pseudo-diagnostic weighting regression
finding: In the ACH group, the final probability moved with the differential consistency score. But the intercept was positive: evidence that was non-diagnostic (same consistency for both hypotheses) still moved judgments. Non-diagnostic evidence carried about 32 percent of the weight of fully diagnostic evidence.
numbers: Regression on differential consistency score: intercept B=0.233, SE=.074, Wald=9.92, p=.002; slope B=0.502, SE=.082, Wald=37.48, p<.001; R2=.055. Robustness coding (C=1, CC=2): intercept B=0.522, slope B=1.20, R2=.072, about 30 percent.
limits: Only measured in the ACH condition, so there is no control comparison on this metric. R2 is small. The 30 to 32 percent figure depends on the scoring of C and CC.
agent_relevance: Gives a measurable target: feed an LLM items with identical likelihood under both hypotheses and check whether its posterior moves. Our SUBFIELDS note already asks this.

source: Karvetski and Mandel (2020), subadditivity and reliability results
finding: Judged P(H1)+P(H2) was below 1 in both conditions, more so when the evidence was stronger. ACH did not fix this. Isomorphic cases with the same evidence structure still gave different answers.
numbers: Subadditivity bias by support: low .13, medium .18, high .21; support effect F=5.04, p<.001; r(225)=.29 overall. Method effect F=1.52, p=.22. 10.1 percent of participants had an undefined Bayesian posterior; 31.7 percent had a probability set to .9999 or .0001.
limits: Bias measured as deviation of the pair sum from 1. Complementary-hypothesis task only.
agent_relevance: Supports G5: probabilities over exclusive hypotheses should be normalised by code, not read as given by the model.

source: Dhami, Belton, De Werd, Hadzhieva and Wicke (2024) Effects of task structure and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation, Cogn Res Princ Implic
finding: Study 1: how the evidence is laid out changes the strategy people use. Hypotheses in rows (HypRow) led to fewer choices of the consistency-favoured hypothesis than ACH-style columns or text. Study 2: Dutch military analysts and cadets mostly (66 percent) balanced consistent and inconsistent evidence.
numbers: Study 1 N=161 (55/51/55). Task 1 chose consistency-favoured A: HypCol 61.8%, HypRow 39.2%, HypText 67.3%; chi2(2)=9.43, p=.009. Credibility switch: 77/78/75%, p=.927. Study 2 N=62: BAL 66.1%, CONS 19.4%, INCONS 14.5%. Credibility sensitivity BAL 98%, CONS 72.7%, INCONS 33.3%. Mean absolute deviation from additivity 15.42 (Study 2), 91.9% nonadditive.
limits: Two hypotheses, 12 items, C/CC/I/II codes. Study 1 sample was 90.1% female non-analysts. Study 2 is a single group, no control. Coherence and CRT did not separate better from worse performers. Only the first 100,000 characters were read.
agent_relevance: Presentation format moves the weighing strategy, so the order and layout the agent sees for evidence is a design choice. The ACH-style matrix gave no gain in credibility sensitivity.

source: Otzipka and Volbert (2026) ACH and expert witness testimony: counteracting adversarial allegiance, PLoS One
finding: Online 2x3 experiment: ACH instruction vs control, crossed with retaining party. ACH (list evidence, mark +/-/0 per hypothesis, drop items scored the same under all, favour fewest inconsistent) did not change credibility ratings or evidence selection.
numbers: N=159 psychologists and students (after exclusions). Credibility: method F(1,153)=.21, p=.649, partial eta2=.001. Evidence Score: method F=1.79, p=.183. Allegiance on Evidence Score: retaining party F=3.12, p=.047; defense vs accessory prosecution diff -.19, 95% CI [-.37, -.00].
limits: Strong exclusions (78 failed knowledge questions, 18 failed attention checks). Participants were students, not working experts. The matrix ratings themselves were not analysed. Only the first 100,000 characters were read.
agent_relevance: Another null result for ACH as a debiasing step; the diagnosticity-pruning step alone does not remove bias that comes from who asked the question.

source: Mandel and Tetlock (2018) Correcting judgment correctives in national security intelligence, Front Psychol
finding: Argues ACH leaves too much to the analyst. 'Consistency' can mean P(E|H), P(H|E), necessity or plausibility, and the common reading is representativeness. Mandel et al. (2018) found ACH-trained analysts more prone to unpacking (coherence-violating) effects than untrained peers. Heuer said that if tests failed he would 'stick with common sense'.
numbers: No sample sizes or effect sizes given for the cited unpacking result. Admiralty codes: analysts' agreement fell as source reliability and information credibility ratings became incongruent.
quote: The meaning of consistency is left up to the analyst to interpret.
limits: Perspective article, not a new experiment. The unpacking study is cited, not reported.
agent_relevance: A clear warning: if we ask the model for 'consistency', the word is ambiguous. Ask for P(E|H) with a stated reference class, and compute the ratio in code.

source: Crupi and Girotto (2014) From is to ought, and back: how normative concerns foster progress in reasoning research, Front Psychol
finding: Describes the pseudodiagnosticity task (Doherty et al. 1979; Kern and Doherty 1982): two equiprobable hypotheses h and not-h, evidence e with P(e|h)=65%, choose one more likelihood from P(e|not-h), P(f|h), P(f|not-h). The classical reading calls choosing P(f|h) irrational. Crupi, Tentori and Lombardi (2009) argued the modal choice can be optimal for a Bayesian, so the 'bias' may be a misapplied norm. Tweney et al. (2010) disputed that.
numbers: Task has one fixed likelihood of 65 percent and three options. The article gives no response percentages.
limits: Second-hand review of the original experiments. No numbers for the 2009 reanalysis in this text.
agent_relevance: Whether a choice is 'pseudodiagnostic' depends on the normative model. Our code should compute expected information gain (see a17), not rely on the label.

source: Crupi, Tentori and Lombardi (2009) Pseudodiagnosticity revisited, Psychological Review 116
finding: Formal reanalysis: with the usual presentation, asking for P(f|h) can be Bayes-rational under some assumptions, so the classical 'bias' label may be a misapplied norm. Not opened (paywalled); the claim comes from a11 and background.
numbers: Not verified in this session.
limits: Not read. Treat as a pointer only.
agent_relevance: Reason to prefer an explicit EIG calculation over a fixed rule like 'always ask the contrast question'.

source: Doherty, Mynatt, Tweney and Schiavo (1979) Pseudodiagnosticity, Acta Psychologica 43; Kern and Doherty (1982) Pseudodiagnosticity in an idealized medical problem-solving environment, J Med Educ 57
finding: Founding experiments: people shown data on one hypothesis tended to ask for more data on the same hypothesis, not the matching data on the rival. Kern and Doherty ran it with medical problem solvers. Not opened. Exact choice percentages not verified here.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Not read in this session. Percentages must be filled from the original before use.
agent_relevance: The agent's S7 test choice is the same problem: from candidates, pick the probe whose answer differs between rivals.

source: Wolf, Gruppen and Billi (1988) Use of the competing-hypotheses heuristic to reduce pseudodiagnosticity, J Med Educ 63
finding: A training study: a competing-hypotheses heuristic was tested as a fix for pseudodiagnosticity in medical students. Only the title and venue were seen in a database list. Result not verified.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Not read.
agent_relevance: Candidate evidence for whether a scaffold step reduces the bias in people. Check the paper before citing.

source: Broder, Scharf, Jekel, Glockner and Franke (2021) Salience effects in information acquisition: no evidence for a top-down coherence influence, Mem Cogn 49
finding: Three studies of which information people search for in a stock task. A bottom-up salience effect on search was found; the predicted top-down coherence (indirect salience) effect was not. The discussion lists pseudodiagnosticity, positive testing and leader-focused search together as search biases (Doherty et al. 1979).
numbers: N=80 (Exp 1), N=80 (Exp 2), N=90 (Exp 3; n=31/30/29), 224 trials each. Mean attraction search score .32, .498, .38. Indirect salience effect pooled t(249)=1.51, p=.13.
limits: Search in a stock-information board, not hypothesis testing with likelihoods. Only the first 100,000 characters of the page were read, so the introduction's pseudodiagnosticity numbers were not available.
agent_relevance: Which information gets looked at is partly driven by what stands out. Our probe list should be built by code, not by whatever the model finds salient.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: uncertainty-aware planning enhances information seeking in LLMs (NeurIPS)
finding: Picks the next question by expected information gain over a candidate set. The model simulates answers, code scores the entropy drop, and rewards are propagated up a short tree. This is a computed diagnosticity score, not a model opinion.
numbers: IG = entropy before minus expected entropy after the yes/no split. Average success-rate gain 38.1 percent over direct prompting across 5 datasets and 5 LLMs; Llama3-70B +46.6; vs CoT-SC +33.8, vs Reflexion +29.9, vs adapted ToT +12.4. GPT-4 on DX closed-set 97.0%; MedDG 88.0%; troubleshooting 43.7% to 67.3%. Examples: Claude-3-Opus 20Q Common closed-set 52.3 to 66.7; Gemini-1.5-Pro MedDG closed-set 51.4 to 81.4.
limits: Closed-set (candidates given) gains are larger than open-set. GPT-4 plays the answerer. Gains are relative to direct prompting. Simulation depth limited to three steps for cost.
agent_relevance: Direct support for S7 as code-computed information gain. The closed-set condition matches our case where candidates come from S3.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM: intelligent information gathering with LLMs and Bayesian experimental design (ICLR 2026)
finding: Chooses each query to maximise expected information gain over a hypothesis distribution built from the LLM's own predictive distribution, with filtering of hypotheses that conflict with answers. It beats prompting-only question writing and a 'split the hypotheses evenly' baseline.
numbers: 20 Questions, end-of-game success, 100 targets each. Animals: GPT-4o-mini Prompt-Only 44, Split 78, CoT 55, BED-LLM 88; GPT-4o 45/83/62/93; Llama-3.1-8B 8/49/19/63; Mistral-Large 33/85/35/95; Qwen2.5-72B 45/87/51/95. Celebrities: GPT-4o 45/63/63/86; Mistral-Large 19/63/42/91. Things: GPT-4o 34/40/49/64; Llama-3.1-8B 10/12/10/26. Ablations on Animals, GPT-4o: marginal entropy 88, data-estimation 70, ICL beliefs 25, implicit max 70.
limits: Answerer is another LLM, so answers are noisy. 'Split' is a strong baseline built with BED-LLM's own filtering. Single run per cell on 100 targets. Task has a clean answer set. Standard errors were garbled in extraction and are omitted.
agent_relevance: Shows full EIG beats a pure 'split' rule when the answerer is noisy. Plain CoT adds little (about +10 points) next to a computed objective (about +40).

source: Gandhi, Li, Goodyear, ... and Goodman (2025) BoxingGym: benchmarking progress in automated experimental design and model discovery
finding: Ten simulated-world environments where an agent chooses experiments, then predicts. Experiment quality is scored by expected information gain (nested Monte Carlo) and an EIG regret against the best design. Models are weak at both design and discovery. Adding an explicit statistical model did not reliably help.
numbers: EIG(d) = E over outcomes of [entropy of parameters before minus after]. Six LLMs tested (GPT-4o, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Qwen-2.5 7B and 32B, OpenThinker 7B and 32B). GPT-4o had the lowest EIG regret and good prediction. Qwen-32B had higher EIG regret despite good prediction. Box's Apprentice did not consistently beat plain GPT-4o and favoured overly simple forms.
limits: Environments are generative models, so EIG is computable only because the simulator is known. Per-environment error tables were not read in full.
agent_relevance: Gives a measure: score the agent's chosen probe by EIG regret. Good prediction does not imply good test choice, so both need separate checks.

source: Li, Kim and Wang (2025) QuestBench: can LLMs ask the right question to acquire information in reasoning tasks?
finding: Underspecified tasks solvable by asking exactly one question (missing variable). The model must pick the question that resolves it. Models do well on math versions but poorly on logic and planning. Solving the full problem is not enough to know the right question.
numbers: Logic-Q and Planning-Q accuracy only 40 to 50 percent; GSM-Q and GSME-Q above 80 percent for the best models (a reported easy-subset figure: 84.05% GSM-Q, 99.39% GSME-Q).
limits: Tables were garbled in the text extraction; only headline figures are used. Multiple-choice questions, not free generation.
agent_relevance: Identifying the discriminating question is a separate skill from solving. S7 should not assume it follows from S4 or S8 ability.

source: Ling (2026) From hindsight to foresight: dissecting clinical evidence acquisition in LLMs (preprint)
finding: Models diagnose well with the full record and when told in hindsight which evidence matters, but poorly when they must ask for evidence step by step. The gap is in choosing and getting the right evidence, not in knowledge.
numbers: Ten models; eligible-pair-weighted accuracy: Fullsight 91.0%, prospective Foresight 74.2%. Primary cohort N=181, k=3 requests: Foresight 33.1% vs matched hindsight 73.5%, gap 40.3 points (95% CI 32.6 to 48.6). Only 58.7% of request slots gave a new fact; 25.3% repeated a known fact; 16.0% matched nothing. Same-set reranking lifted 34.3% to 43.7% (+9.3); replacing the set with the hindsight-selected set gave 70.3% (+26.7).
limits: Single preprint under review, one clinical case source. The 33.1% and 74.2% Foresight figures come from different cohorts and denominators.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that evidence selection, not weighing, is the bottleneck. Backs a code-built list of discriminating probes at S7.

source: Qiu, Sha, Allen, Kim, Linzen and van Steenkiste (2026) Bayesian teaching enables probabilistic reasoning in LLMs
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs update beliefs poorly versus an exact Bayesian assistant: accuracy often plateaus after one round. Fine-tuning to mimic the Bayesian assistant's predictions fixes much of it and generalises to new tasks.
numbers: Flight-recommendation task, 624 simulated users, 5 rounds; human subset 48. Gemma 2, Llama 3, Qwen 2.5 (7B to 70B). Bayesian-tuned models agree with the Bayesian assistant about 80 percent of the time, more than original or oracle-tuned models.
limits: Preference inference, not hypothesis discrimination. Needs fine-tuning, which we do not do. Humans also fell short of the Bayesian ceiling.
agent_relevance: LLMs do not accumulate likelihoods across rounds. Keep the running posterior in code, not in the context.

source: Lampinen, Dasgupta, Chan, ... and Hill (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: On the Wason selection task, language models score above chance but worse on abstract than realistic rules, like humans. Human accuracy was not above chance overall; slow humans did better on realistic rules.
numbers: Realistic vs arbitrary advantage: Chinchilla, PaLM 2-L, GPT-3.5 and humans all z>2.2, p<0.03; PaLM 2-M and Flan-PaLM 2 marginal (z about 1.78, p about .08). Slowest 15% of humans (over 80 seconds) were above chance only on Realistic.
limits: Wason is a card-selection logic task, not diagnosticity weighing. Percent-correct figures are in a figure and were not extracted.
agent_relevance: Test choice quality depends on content familiarity, so S7 probes should be phrased in the domain's terms.

source: Zou and Xu (2026) WORTH Benchmark: evidence discovery under not-fully-cooperative information (pilot)
finding: Models read mystery narratives and pick key clue sentences. Clue hits and participant judgments came apart. In one episode most runs chose the same wrong suspects and picked suspicion-leaning clue sentences far more than exonerating ones.
numbers: 70 runs, 67 scorable. Episode 02: 37 scorable runs, 31 chose the same incorrect participant set; adjacent suspicion-oriented sentences selected 25 times, exoneration-oriented 0 times; 28 of 37 runs (75.7%) had negative scores.
limits: Pilot, two episodes, no human comparison, no stable ranking claimed.
agent_relevance: A clean case of models taking evidence that points one way and skipping the discriminating exculpatory item, which is what a diagnosticity step must catch.

source: Zhao, Zhao, Yu, Zhang and Li (2025) AgentCDM: collaborative decision-making via ACH-inspired structured reasoning
finding: Uses ACH as a protocol for a decision agent that reads several agents' answers: each answer is a hypothesis, evidence items are rated against each, the matrix is revised, then a conclusion is drawn. A two-stage training removes the scaffold. It beat plain voting rules.
numbers: MMLU, MMLU-Pro, ARC-Challenge accuracy. Voting methods changed accuracy by about +0.6 to -0.4 points on average. ACH protocol with a fixed Qwen-7B-Instruct decision agent: all-average about +2.3; trained AgentCDM about +7.0 to +7.8. MMLU-Pro 65.2% vs Qwen-7B-R1 58.0%.
limits: Table parsed from PDF text and partly garbled; deltas are approximate. Trained model, multi-agent answer aggregation, not evidence diagnosticity in the strict sense. No matched-token single-agent baseline. Conflicts with our G9 view that multi-agent gains are mostly extra sampling.
agent_relevance: Only weak evidence for ACH as a prompt; the large gain needs training. Do not adopt as a debate-like step.

source: Mellers, McCoy, Lu and Tetlock (2024) Human and algorithmic predictions in geopolitical forecasting, Perspect Psychol Sci
finding: Review of IARPA tournament findings. Humans are sensitive to irrelevant cues such as pseudodiagnosticity; algorithms help most by aggregating and reducing noise. Training raised accuracy about 6 to 11 percent; more than half of accuracy gains came from noise reduction.
numbers: Grove et al. (2000) statistical advantage d=0.12. Teams beat independent forecasters in each of four years. Superforecasters were the top 2 percent.
limits: Review; the pseudodiagnosticity mention is a single remark, with no data.
agent_relevance: Noise reduction by structure is the cheaper win: fix the evidence-handling procedure rather than hope for better judgment.

source: Wason (1960) On the failure to eliminate hypotheses in a conceptual task, QJEP 12; Klayman and Ha (1987) Confirmation, disconfirmation and information in hypothesis testing, Psych Rev 94
finding: Not opened. Background: Wason's 2-4-6 shows people test with sequences their hypothesis predicts. Klayman and Ha argued the positive test strategy is not the same as confirmation bias and is often good when a hypothesis is true of a minority of cases, but fails when the true rule is broader than the guess. Heuer's version (a03) gives the 6 of 29 figure.
numbers: Only Heuer's second-hand numbers (6 of 29; 0 of 51) are confirmed.
limits: Not read in this session. Do not cite details beyond what a03 supports.
agent_relevance: Clarifies that 'seek disconfirming evidence' is the wrong rule; the right rule is 'seek the probe where rivals differ'.

source: Oaksford and Chater (1994) A rational analysis of the selection task as optimal data selection, Psychol Rev 101; Nelson (2005) Finding useful questions, Psychol Rev 112
finding: Not opened. Background: both propose that good tests are chosen by expected information gain over hypotheses given prior probabilities. Oaksford and Chater recast the Wason task this way (a rarity assumption). Nelson compared diagnosticity measures such as probability gain, information gain, KL distance, impact and likelihood-ratio diagnosticity. Crupi and Girotto (a11) describe the first.
numbers: Not verified in this session.
limits: Not read. Details of Nelson's ranking of measures must be checked before use.
agent_relevance: These are the formal models behind a code-side S7: enumerate probes, compute the expected entropy drop under the current posterior, choose the max.

source: Good (1950) Probability and the Weighing of Evidence; Fischhoff and Beyth-Marom (1983) Hypothesis evaluation from a Bayesian perspective, Psych Rev 90
finding: Not opened. Background: the diagnostic value of evidence E for H1 against H2 is the likelihood ratio P(E|H1)/P(E|H2); on the log scale evidence adds up. Fischhoff and Beyth-Marom use this as the normative yardstick and catalogue how people depart from it. Heuer's ch. 8 matrix is a coarse version of this ratio.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Not read. The tie-in to Heuer is my inference, not a quote.
agent_relevance: The core computation the program can do: log-likelihood-ratio per item, summed in code under a stated independence assumption.
